titel: Black Monday 1987 and the Japanese bubble
kurz: Why the largest one-day loss in stock market history was recovered in less than two years, while the Japanese stock market needed thirty-four years to recover after its peak at the end of the 1980s.

bloecke.md:
Just over two years lie between 19 October 1987 and 29 December 1989. Neither day is missing from any chronology of financial crises, and they stand for two opposite kinds of crisis.

On the first of the two days, the Dow Jones lost 508 points or 22.6%, more than on any other trading day in its history. On the second, the Nikkei 225 closed at 38,915.87 points, a record that barely made headlines. An investor who stayed invested in 1987 had made up the damage after 23 months. Buyers of Japanese shares on 29 December 1989, by contrast, had to wait 34 years and two months until the index reached the same level again.

A crash arises from the mechanics of trading, a bubble from inflated prices. Only after a bubble does the recovery take decades.

## Portfolio insurance and programme trading

In the mid-1980s, [[Portfolio insurance|portfolio insurance]] was Wall Street's best-selling risk product. The technique was used to protect large portfolios against price losses and was therefore the opposite of speculation. The idea comes from option theory. Instead of buying an expensive put option, you replicate it. If the market falls, you sell index futures; if it rises, you buy them back. This costs only fees, as long as someone is buying on the other side.

On 19 October 1987, these buyers were missing. The rule “sell when prices fall” had been programmed identically into hundreds of portfolios. It demanded ever larger sales the further the market had already fallen. Every sale pushed the price down, and every lower price triggered the next sell order. [[Programme trading]] turned a correction into a self-reinforcing fall in prices. The sales followed a mathematical rule and were not based on any new assessment of corporate earnings.

A hedge that everyone uses at the same time amplifies price losses instead of limiting them. As soon as enough market participants follow the same automatic rule, reducing risk turns into a downward spiral.

The losses spread to other stock exchanges for technical, not economic, reasons. In October 1987, Hong Kong lost 45.5%, Australia 41.8%, the UK 26.4% and Canada 22.5%. The back-calculated DAX closed on 19 October down 9.39% at 1,321.61 points; the index itself only existed from 1988. None of these economies had received bad news over the preceding weekend. Investors who needed liquidity in New York sold whatever could be sold.

This shows a limit to diversification. In panics, correlations approach one, and markets then move almost in unison. The cause is sales forced by margin calls, which have nothing to do with assessments of individual securities. Diversification protects against the failure of individual companies, but least of all against a liquidity shock on a single day.

Normally, arbitrage keeps the futures contract and the cash market in line. If the future is too cheap, a trader buys it and sells the underlying shares. On Black Monday, this link stopped working. At times, the futures traded well below the calculated index value because they were the only way to sell quickly at all. At the same time, the index level was unreliable, because for many individual shares no price could be established for hours owing to the flood of orders. An arbitrageur wanting to step in would have been trading against prices that did not exist. Liquidity therefore depends less on the individual security than on the market situation at the given moment.

bloecke.md:
## Limited consequences of the crash

The price fall did not spread to the credit system. Unlike in 1929, no significant part of the banking system depended on securities-backed loans, and unlike in 2008, there was no chain of liabilities behind the falling securities. The central bank declared the following morning that it would supply the system with liquidity. This answered the only acute question, namely whether brokers and clearing houses would survive the day.

From its high on 25 August to its low on 4 December 1987, the S&P 500 lost a total of 33.5%. On 26 July 1989, it was back at its old level, 701 calendar days after the peak. It ended calendar year 1987 up 5.81% including dividends. For German investors, the result looked different. The MSCI World lost 5.3% in Deutsche Mark terms in 1987 and regained 38.8% in 1988. The exchange rate had a bigger effect than the crash.

The New York Stock Exchange introduced [[Circuit breaker|circuit breakers]] in 1988. Today, a fall in the S&P 500 of 7% or 13% halts US trading for 15 minutes, and at 20% the trading day ends. In Xetra trading, volatility interruptions perform the same task for individual securities. If the next execution price would leave a predefined price range, the system briefly switches to an auction. Neither procedure prevents price losses. They enforce a pause that also applies to orders that machines have already generated.

## The bubble in Tokyo

In 1989, the enthusiasm for Japan was based on the country's situation at the time and not on hopes for the future. Japan was running large export surpluses, its industry was considered superior, and its banks were among the largest in the world. This description was accurate, yet share prices were still too high.

At its peak, the price-to-earnings ratio of the Japanese market was around 80. The long-term average of developed stock markets is more like 15 to 20. One square metre in Tokyo's Ginza business district cost 30 million yen. According to contemporary estimates, the grounds of the Imperial Palace were worth more than all the real estate in California. This is not an official value, but it is a useful indication of the mood at the time.

The bubble was ended by a decision of the central bank and not by an external event. Between May 1989 and August 1990, the Bank of Japan raised its key interest rate from 2.5% to 6.0%, expressly to curb asset prices. The Nikkei 225 fell to 7,608 points by April 2003 and reached its low of 7,054.98 points in March 2009, 81.9% below its peak. It did not surpass its 1989 level until 22 February 2024, at 39,098.68 points.

bloecke.md:
## Price return index and total return index

The figure of 34 years is correct but misleading. The Nikkei 225 is a [[Price return index|price return index]]; dividends are not included in it. The DAX, by contrast, is a total return index in which distributions are notionally reinvested. The DAX itself shows how large the difference is. Both versions started at 1,000 points on 30 December 1987. At the end of 2025, the total return index stood at 24,490 points and the price return index at 9,175 points. This corresponds to 8.8% versus 6.0% a year, that is, around 2.8 percentage points a year from dividends alone.

A Japanese investor who reinvested the dividends was therefore back in profit earlier than the index level suggests. How much earlier depends on the dividend yield and on deflation. The sources used do not provide a reliable year for this, so it is not estimated here. This does not change the order of magnitude: the recovery took decades.

Two investors each invest €10,000 on 29 December 1989 (Deutsche Marks at the time, calculated in euros throughout here).

- Investor A buys the home market, in this case the Nikkei 225. On 22 February 2024, the index stands 0.47% above the entry level. €10,000 has become €10,047, without dividends, because the index does not include any.
- Investor B diversifies globally. Measured as a net return in Deutsche Marks and euros, the MSCI World achieved a cumulative 10.6 times its starting value from 1990 to 2023, that is, 7.2% a year. This turned €10,000 into around €106,000.

The comparison has a weakness that needs to be kept in mind. The MSCI figure includes reinvested dividends after foreign withholding tax; the Nikkei figure includes none. With dividends, A would be better off than shown, but this does not change the order of magnitude. German flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer) and fund costs have not been deducted from either figure.

## Country weights in the world index

In 1989, Japan was not a niche market. At times, Japanese shares accounted for something in the order of four tenths of the MSCI World. At the end of August 2026, the figure is 5.78%, while the USA accounts for 72.14%. Investors who invested “in developed markets” at the time therefore put a large part of their money into the bubble. This is one drawback of an index weighted by market capitalisation, because it contains the most of whatever has become the most expensive.

Equally valid is the objection that the same mechanism automatically reduces the weight afterwards, without anyone having to recognise the turning point. A world index recovers from its bubbles; a single country does not necessarily do so within an investor's lifetime. This is the difference between [[Home market bias|home market bias]] and diversification.

The statement “shares always come back” has so far held true for broadly diversified world indices. For individual countries, it does not hold within a period you can plan for, and for individual shares not at all. A portfolio with 70% in the DAX structurally carries the same risk that Japanese investors unknowingly took on in 1989, only in a smaller market.

## Tax consequences of weak stock market years

For accumulating funds, the [[Advance lump sum (Vorabpauschale)|advance lump sum (Vorabpauschale)]] under Section 18 InvStG (Investment Tax Act) taxes a notional minimum return every year. The formula is: advance lump sum = redemption price on the first valuation day of the year × base interest rate (Basiszins) × 0.7 (base return, Basisertrag), less distributions. However, the advance lump sum is capped. The amount applied is never more than the increase in value during the year, so in a sideways or loss-making year it is zero.

The Bundesbank derives the base interest rate from the yield curve, and the Federal Ministry of Finance publishes it (Section 18(4) InvStG). For 2026 it is 3.20%, and the advance lump sum is only charged in January 2027 (Section 18(3) InvStG). In the following example, the redemption price on 2 January 2026 is €10,000, it is unchanged at the end of the year, and there is no distribution. The base return is 10,000 × 3.20% × 0.7 = €224, but the advance lump sum is still €0. Amounts applied reduce the capital gain on a later sale in full (Section 19(1) InvStG). They are therefore a prepayment and not an additional tax.

In crisis years, two rules regularly come as a surprise. First, under Section 20(6) sentence 4 EStG (Income Tax Act), losses from the sale of shares may only be offset against gains from share sales. Investors who sell individual shares at a loss in a panic and realise ETF gains at the same time cannot offset one against the other. Second, the nominal gain is taxed; Section 20 EStG makes no provision for inflation adjustment. For equity funds, the 30% partial exemption (Teilfreistellung) under Section 20(1) InvStG mitigates this effect.

1. Compare the country share in your portfolio with its weight in the world index. This is not about poorer prospects; however, a slump in the home market often hits your job, your property and your pension at the same time.
2. Check automatic sell rules. A stop-loss order is the private version of portfolio insurance. It is triggered when everyone is selling and is executed at the next tradable price, not at the stop price.
3. Get to know the loss pots before you need them. Which pot absorbs which loss determines the tax burden for the year.

mitnehmen: A crash that arises from the mechanics of trading is recovered within months to a few years; a bubble built on excessive valuations and credit only after decades.
In 1987, the Dow fell by 22.6% in a single day, yet the year still ended with a gain of 5.81% for the S&P 500.
The Nikkei 225 took from 29 December 1989 to 22 February 2024, that is, 34 years and two months, to reach a new high.
The recovery required rises disproportionately: after minus 33.5%, plus 50% is needed, and after minus 81.9%, plus 452%.
Investing in a single developed market is not diversification, even if that market at times makes up four tenths of the world index.

begriffe.text: Hedging technique that replicates a put option by automatically selling index futures when prices fall. When many market participants follow the same rule, it has a procyclical effect and amplifies the crash, as on 19 October 1987.

Rule-based trading halt on a stock exchange after a specified fall in prices. They have existed in the USA since 1988. Today, trading is suspended for 15 minutes when the S&P 500 is down 7% or 13%, and at minus 20% the trading day ends.

Index that reflects only price changes, without dividends. The Nikkei 225, S&P 500 and Dow Jones are usually quoted as price return indices, whereas the DAX is quoted as a total return index with notionally reinvested distributions. For the DAX, the difference is around 2.8 percentage points a year.

The tendency to invest a disproportionately large amount in shares of your own country. It increases cluster risk because your job, property and portfolio follow the same business cycle. Japan in 1989 is the most expensive documented case.

Notional minimum return on funds that is taxed every year under Section 18 InvStG. It is the base return (redemption price at the start of the year × base interest rate × 0.7, at most the increase in value plus distributions for the year) less distributions, and it therefore also arises for distributing funds if the distributions are below the base return. The base interest rate for 2026 is 3.20%.
